title: Template wobble catalogue (scratch)
content:
Quick notes: trying to capture a small, messy catalog of template "wobbles" — i.e., small structural or wording changes to otherwise identical templates that produce qualitatively different model behavior. This is personal scratch; leave open questions and short reproducible examples.

Goal
- Build a tiny corpus of minimal diffs that cause output drift. Use these as regression test inputs for prompt-stability evaluations and for the prompt-bank (see PR 412).

Definition: wobble = a small syntactic/lexical change in a template that shifts distribution of high-level outputs (style, facts, hallucination rate, step ordering, refusal rate). Not necessarily catastrophic, but stable enough to be measurable across runs.

Quick hypotheses
- Wobble often happens at instruction boundaries: where role lines meet exemplars, or when an explicit constraint moves from header into exemplar.
- Politeness markers (please, kindly) shift verbosity but sometimes also alter whether model refuses tasks.
- The presence/absence of an extraneous punctuation (colon vs dash) at the end of a directive can flip whether the model enumerates steps or writes prose.

Experiment log (seeded runs)
- Model: open-variant-900M-qual (test harness); temp=0.2; 5-shot unless noted.
- Input set id: wobble-experiments-2026-03-10 (local harness).

1) Instruction boundary shift- Base template A: 
  System: You are an assistant that writes concise debugging steps.
  User: Here is a bug report: <BUG>
  Example 1: Bug: app crashes when saving. Steps: 1) reproduce 2) gather logs 3) propose fix.
  Prompt: Given the bug report, list prioritized debugging steps.

  Variant A1 (move constraint into example): "Example 1: Bug: app crashes. Steps (concise): 1)..."
  Observation: Variant produced 3 enumerated steps, terse. Base template produced a paragraph first, then numbered list.
  Takeaway: shifting 'concise' into exemplar bias the model to keep each item short.

2) Politeness wobble- Base: "Please summarize the article in 3 bullets."
  Variant: "Summarize the article in 3 bullets."
  Observation: 'Please' => slightly longer bullets, more hedging. Removing please => more direct, factual. Unexpectedly 'please' increased use of soft qualifiers ("It seems...").

3) Punctuation at directive end- Base: "List the steps to reproduce:" (colon)
  Variant: "List the steps to reproduce." (period)
  Observation: Colon leads to enumerated list more often. Period leads to inline sentence or a short paragraph. Small but consistent across model runs.

4) Exemplar role inversion (few-shot order)- 3-shot set where examples alternate between "bug => fix" and "symptom => triage". When I reverse the order of exemplars so all "bug=>fix" are first then the mixed ones, it biases the model to output 'fix-first' templates (i.e., proposed fix appears before root cause analysis).

Micro-examples to copy into harness
- Minimal prompt pair (compare A & B):
  A:
  "You are an assistant that explains policies.
  Explain the refund policy for a customer who bought on 2025-10-01:"
  B:
  "You are an assistant that explains policies.
  Explain the refund policy for a customer who bought on 2025-10-01. Please be short:"
  Result: B more likely to produce an explicit eligibility line followed by a short conclusion. A is more verbose and mixes procedural steps in the same paragraph.

Failure modes observed
- Silent mode switch: a single adjective redirects style (e.g., 'technical' vs 'plain'). Sometimes model flips to stepwise when 'technical' is present (counterintuitive).
- Over-enumeration: colon + exemplar + polite qualifier => model invents too many micro-steps. Need to watch token budget.
- Rare hallucination spike when exemplar includes a date or ID; model may fabricate a related "precedent" event. Likely priming effect from example wording.

Ideas for small canonical tests (that we can add to unit suite)
- punctuation-enum-test: directive with colon vs period vs nothing -> measure fraction of outputs that start with a numbered list.
- please-hedge-test: with vs without 'please' -> measure hedging tokens (% of tokens matching hedging lexicon).
- exemplar-placement-test: move constraint from header to exemplar -> measure average sentence length per item.

Quick templates for the prompt-bank (candidate entries)
- "enum-seed" (3-shot): controlled exemplars that encourage enumeration. Keep one variant with colon, one with period.
- "please-vs-direct" (2-shot): same content, different politeness marker.
- "constraint-in-exemplar" (2-shot): show effect of moving constraint.

Notes to self / TODOs
- Convert 10 largest-wobble examples into JSON test cases for the harness. Prioritize those that show consistent delta across 10 seeds.
- Talk to Luca about adding 'wobble' metrics to Console: fraction-of-list-starts, average-item-length, hedge-token-rate.
- Check with SRE if prompt seeds hitting dedicated infra show different wobble characteristics (maybe runtime quantization impacts generation ordering). Add a small dedicated run next week.

Open questions / experiments to run
- Is wobble persistent across model sizes? Run the same tests on small/medium/large. My intuition: small models exaggerate differences; larger ones smooth them. Need data.
- Does shutting off streaming vs streaming affect list detection? Observed slight timing-based truncation in one run.
- Are wobble effects correlated with tokenization boundary placement? (e.g., whether a colon attaches to previous token).

Scratch: example failure case to reproduce and file as ticket
- Observed: a support-script generator template where moving the word 'required' from header to exemplar made the generator omit a required field in output. Repro steps: compare templates X and Y (attached to PR 412). If reproducible, create JIRA-4521 with minimal repro and attach logs.

Packing note: keep this doc light. When I have 10 stable cases, move to prompt-bank as canonical entries and write a short explainer doc (public-facing internal page) for product/solutions teams: "Why tiny prompt changes change output in the wild".

Personal heuristics (from closed-loop tinkering)
- When you need deterministic enumeration, include a numbered exemplar rather than relying on punctuation alone.
- If style drift is the problem, anchor both the header and an exemplar with the same style adjective. Redundancy helps.
- Add an explicit example of refusal mode if you need consistent safe refusals (show rather than tell).

End scratch.

-- eeb (Evelyn)
